title: How do you change a company's direction with one prototype?
subtitle: User research that overturned an executive assumption at a print-on-demand platform
team: Team of 3, growing into implementation teams, Leipzig

sections.headline: How do you change a company's direction with one prototype?
sections.subtext: The leadership vision was a 60-second automated journey. User research said the opposite. This is how the research won.

sections.headline: The starting point
sections.content:
Spreadshirt was running on an assumption that felt obviously right at the top: shop owners want speed. The leadership vision was a 60-second journey, pick a template, let it customise itself, ship. Efficient, scalable, clean.

The company had tried to redesign the seller experience twice before, and failed both times. I was brought in to lead the third attempt. I started with one question: what if the assumption was wrong?

sections.quote: The t-shirt designer is the most uplifting experience I have all day.
sections.attribution: A shop owner, during a user interview
sections.context: The sentence that changed the product strategy

sections.headline: What the research found
sections.content:
I went and talked to shop owners. Not surveys, not analytics: conversations.

What they told me contradicted the leadership vision outright. They did not want the design process automated away. For them the t-shirt designer was the best part of their day, not friction to get through. They valued creative control over speed. The creative process was the product.

That was not a small note in the margins. It meant the entire 60-second automation strategy was pointed the wrong way.

sections.headline: Making the research undeniable
sections.content:
The data said one thing and executive intuition said another, and two earlier attempts had already failed. A presentation was not going to move that.

So I built a prototype: a mobile version of the t-shirt designer, put directly into users' hands. The point was not to prove mobile was technically possible. It was to show that the design experience itself was worth keeping, that it held up, and still felt good, even on a small screen.

images.caption: The one-week mobile prototype: built to show the design experience survives on a small screen.

steps.label: User interviews
steps.description: In-depth conversations with shop owners, which surfaced that the design process was the emotional core of their experience, not friction to remove.

steps.label: A research prototype
steps.description: A mobile t-shirt designer built in Axure RP with the UI designers over one intensive week, made to provoke user feedback, not to ship.

steps.label: Executive workshops
steps.description: Workshops with the executive team and business-unit leadership, presenting findings that contradicted the leadership assumption about automation.

steps.label: User testing
steps.description: Tested the prototype with real users. The response was strongly positive, and showed the full desktop experience could work on mobile.

sections.headline: What changed

metrics.label: Product strategy
metrics.before: A 60-second fully automated journey: design friction removed
metrics.after: Controlled automation: user agency and creative control kept

metrics.label: The redesign project
metrics.after: Completed over nine months; the team grew from three into full implementation teams

metrics.label: Executive buy-in
metrics.value: Leadership backed a direction that contradicted their own original intuition

sections.narrative: The mobile prototype tested well: it showed the design experience could work on a small screen. The larger result was strategic: leadership changed the product approach from full automation to controlled automation. The redesign that had failed twice was finished, over nine months, scaling from a team of three into larger implementation teams.

sections.headline: What I took from it
sections.content:
Data on its own does not change a decision, you have to make it undeniable. When research contradicts leadership intuition, a slide deck will not do it. A prototype that puts users in control will.

It also fixed something for me about strategy: the best product direction does not start from efficiency metrics. It starts from what users actually value. Sometimes the thing you are trying to optimise away is the thing they love most.

executive.summary: Changed a company's product strategy from full automation to controlled automation, by running user research that showed shop owners valued creative control above speed. The prototype tested well; the redesign finished after two prior failures.

narrative.summary: What happens when user research contradicts leadership intuition? The story of how one shop owner's sentence changed a company's product direction.
